Two degrees, B.S. in Dietetics and a B.S. in Nutrition, are available.

Dietetics The Dietetics degree is required of all students planning to become Registered Dietitians.
URI’s Dietetics program is accredited by the Commission on Accreditation Council for Education in Nutrition and Dietetics (ACEND), 120 South Riverside Plaza, Suite 2190, Chicago, IL 60606, 800.877.1600, ext. 5400; https://www.eatrightpro.org/acend/.
Please see the department website for complete program information (https://web.uri.edu/nfs/ ).
The Dietetics major requires 27 credits in sciences (four in general chemistry [CHM 103/105], four in organic chemistry [CHM 124/126], three in biochemistry [CMB 210], 12 in biology [BIO 110/103; 220/221; 222/223], and four in microbiology [CMB 201]), 4 credits in applied general nutrition (NFS 210), 4 credits in introductory professional courses (NFS 110 and 212G); and 41 credits in the concentration including the following courses: NFS 336, 337, 375, 376, 394, 395, 410, 440, 441, 443, 444, 445, and 458 [capstone].

Additionally, MGT 341 is required and COM 100, MTH 103, PSY 113, SOC 100, STA 220, and WRT 104 are required and may be used to fulfill general education requirements.
There are 16-19 credits of free electives.
Students are encouraged to use supporting elective and free elective courses to study disciplines related to the field.
Students must maintain a 3.00 average in all required courses (NFS courses, science courses, and the remaining degree courses), with no less than a C in any one required class, in order to graduate.
A total of 120 credits is required for graduation.
Students will be admitted to the Dietetics degree program after completing a minimum of 31 credits, including BIO 110/103; CHM 103/105, 124; BIO 220/221; NFS 210 or 212G; WRT 104; COM 100; and STA 220.
Students must have earned a 3.00 average in these classes with no less than a C in any one class to be admitted.Students may repeat NFS courses once.
Transfer students, both internal and external, will be admitted to the major on a space available basis through the Waiting for Dietetics program and there is no guarantee that students in the competitive admissions pool will be admitted to the major.

Admission is a two-step process: an initial decision made after the completion of two course sequences, and a second decision made after completion of the major admission requirements.
After completing their B.S. requirements, students can qualify for the professional title of Registered Dietitian by completing supervised practice requirements and passing a national exam.
The supervised practice requirement is met by completing an ACEND-accredited dietetic internship program available to students on a competitive basis nationwide.
Admission to internship programs is highly competitive; students are encouraged to review the latest admission information on the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics website (https://www.eatrightpro.org/acend/students-and-advancing-education/information-for-students).
Internships may be combined with graduate programs in universities leading to an advanced degree.
Students who complete the academic and supervised practice requirements are eligible to take the national registration examination.

THE UNIVERSITY OF RHODE ISLAND Revised 10/2021 Notice of Change form Catalog Description The Department of Chemical Engineering (CHE) offers a curriculum leading to the Bachelor of Science (B.S.) degree in chemical engineering.
The chemical engineering program is accredited by the Engineering Accreditation Commission (EAC) of ABET, Inc. (www.abet.org).
Specializations to the bachelor’s degree are possible by adding a minor.
The department also offers the Master of Science (M.S.) and Doctor of Philosophy (Ph.D.) degrees.
Faculty: Professor Bothun, Chairperson.
Professors Bose, Brown, Gregory, and Lucia; Associate Professors Greenfield and Meenach; Assistant Professors Poling-Skutvik, Roxbury, and Shen; Professors Emeriti Barnett, Crisman, Gray, Knickle, Rivero-Hudec, Rockett, and Rose.
The chemical engineer is concerned with the application and control of processes leading to changes in chemical composition.

These processes are most frequently associated with the production of useful products (chemicals, fuels, metals, foods, pharmaceuticals, paper, plastics, and the like), but also include processes such as removal of toxic components from the blood by an artificial kidney, environmental cleanup, and semiconductor processing.
The chemical engineer’s domain includes more efficient production and use of energy, processing of wastes, and protection of the environment.
Chemical engineers have a strong foundation in chemistry, physics, mathematics, and basic engineering.
Chemical engineering courses include thermodynamics, transport phenomena, mass transfer operations, materials engineering, process dynamics and control, kinetics, and plant design.
The student has the opportunity to operate small-scale equipment and to visit local industry.
Intensive work is undertaken in the solution of complex problems in which economics and optimization of engineering design are emphasized.
Students who graduate with a degree in chemical engineering work in a variety of fields including pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, environmental engineering, materials science, nanotechnology, etc.

The URI chemical engineering major provides flexibility for students to pursue a variety of minors, such as cell and molecular biology, pharmaceutical manufacturing and formulation, business, chemistry, engineering entrepreneurship, environmental engineering, nuclear engineering, and neuroscience.
Department Mission Statement.
We are a community in a common quest to create and distribute chemical engineering knowledge in order to prepare our graduates to be successful leaders and practitioners.

URI’s chemical engineering program is more than just a collection of courses and credit hours whose content reflects the required criteria.
The program has also been carefully designed to prepare students for the profession of chemical engineering through study, experience, and practice.

Through eight specific program goals, the department of chemical engineering at URI seeks to: 1) provide the necessary background in science, particularly chemistry, physics, and advanced mathematics through the study of differential equations, so that students will be able to continue their education in the engineering sciences, with depth of understanding, and learn to apply these subjects to the formulation and solution of engineering problems; 2) provide a broad cross section of fundamental engineering science courses, including some from other engineering disciplines so that our students will acquire an understanding of the way in which chemistry, physics, and mathematics have been and continue to be used to solve important engineering problems relevant to the general chemical engineering and engineering design; 3) provide students with experience in conducting and planning experiments in the modern engineering laboratory, including interfacing experiments with computers as well as interpreting the significance of resulting data and properly reporting results in well-written technical reports; 4) provide experience in the process of original chemical engineering design in the areas of equipment design, process design, and plant design through the process of formulating a design solution to a perceived need and then executing the design and evaluating its performance, including economic considerations and societal impacts if any, along with other related constraints, culminating in both written and oral presentations of results; 5) provide experience with the multifaceted aspects of using computers to solve problems and present results with word processing, spreadsheet, presentation, and professional-level applications software used for design and analysis; and provide for obtaining and using information on the World Wide Web; 6) provide a familiarity with professional issues in chemical engineering, including ethics, issues related to the global economy and to emerging technologies, and fostering of important job-related skills such as improved oral and written communications and experience in working in teams at a number of levels; 7) encourage students to become actively engaged in the student chapter of the American Institute of Chemical Engineers and other student organizations, and to continue these associations after graduation with an emphasis on the importance of lifelong professional development including the desirability of attending graduate school or otherwise obtaining continuing or advanced education; Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) This proposed Certificate in Data Analytics for Accounting Program focuses on developing skills needed in today’s rapidly changing work environment by practicing accountants and those entering the profession who hold a bachelor’s degree in accounting or finance from URI or elsewhere.
It differs from other specialized data analytics programs offered through URI Online.
For example, the Online Graduate Certificate in Data Science is a generalist certificate but it requires a sequence of courses focused on mathematical and computer-based exploration methods.
In contrast, this proposed program offers an applied focus for the accounting profession with modules and examples focused specifically on accounting topics.

The program is composed of four three-credit courses delivered in an accelerated, online format: MBA 500, Statistical Methods for Management (already approved for online delivery) MAC 511, Data Analytics for Accounting (currently offered online as an elective in the MS Accounting Program) MAC 512, Data Analytics for Auditing, a newly offered online course submitted herewith for approval MAC 518, Directed Study in Accounting, a current offering with a structure online-format syllabus for this program submitted herewith MBA 500 and MAC 511 are already approved for delivery online in a 10-week format.

B1.
Explain and quantify the needs addressed by this program, and present evidence that the program fulfills these needs.
Two sources, among many, indicate the need for a data analytics focus among accounting practitioners.
They include: 1) an article by one of the Big 4 audit firms which employs many of our accounting graduates, Ernst & Young (E&Y), (available at https://www.ey.com/en_us/assurance/how-big-data-and-analytics-are-transforming-the-audit); and, 2) an article focused on smaller and mid-tier accounting firms, as well as corporate internal auditing and accounting functions, available at https://www.journalofaccountancy.com/issues/2015/apr/data-analytics-for-auditors.html Together, these publications discuss the relevance and importance of incorporating analytics techniques into accounting practice across the wide spectrum of accounting practice.
EY notes that big data and analytics are enabling auditors to better identify financial reporting, fraud and operational business risks and to deliver a more relevant audit.

Further, the Association of International Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) is proposing changes to the U.S. national CPA exam to include testing of data analytics skills.
Members of the URI Accounting Faculty are not just monitoring these developments: Professor Judy Beckman and Assistant Professor Qi Liu have participated in the process to provide input to and feedback on the changing CPA exam.
Our planned courses for this certificate program meet these changing needs for accounting and auditing practitioners and those entering the profession.
Competitors to this program are shown in the table attached at the end of this document.

There are two primary groups of students expected to enroll in the program: (1) practitioners looking to enhance data analytics skills due to the factors described under B1 above; and, (2) URI undergraduate students graduating with credit hours greater than 120.
For practitioners, we expect that offering a certificate program will provide benefit to those already holding the CPA who need to enhance their data analytics skills.

Those graduating with the bachelors’ degree credits nearing completion of 150 credit hours may enroll in this certificate program.
They otherwise may take a more random selection of electives to complete the 150 credit hours necessary to become CPAs.
Rhode Island and many nearing states require 150 credit hours of education but not a Master’s degree.
Enrolling in the certificate program will provide added benefit to these students beyond the bachelor’s degree and offer demonstrated evidence to employers of enhanced skill attainment.
Further, for these students, the national CPA exam is changing to include a greater emphasis on data analytics in both core knowledge areas and in a specialty track.
This proposed certificate program is designed to support students aiming for the CPA exam in general and a data analytics track in particular.
